title: Assemblies, metadata, and InternalsVisibleTo
hook: Module 01 stopped at “Roslyn emits IL into a DLL.” Interviewers then ask who may see `internal` and how identity is stored. That is metadata, not a C# keyword trivia quiz.

sections.heading: What an assembly actually is
sections.prose: An assembly is the unit the CLR loads: IL, type metadata, and a manifest (name, version, culture, optional public key). A RabbitMQ client NuGet package is one or more assemblies plus a nuspec; it is not a folder of `.cs` files Node would `import`. Identity for binding is the simple name plus version and, when signed, the public key token. Culture matters for satellite resources, not for your typical SQS consumer. Two copies of the same simple name with different versions in one process is a bind failure unless you alias or unify — interviews still call this “DLL hell,” which is imprecise; it is loader policy. Native AOT still starts from assemblies, then closes the world: types that exist only via `Assembly.Load(byte[])` are gone unless you preserved them.

snippets.label: Inspect identity without inventing a plugin host
snippets.explanation: FullName is the bind identity string. Logging it in a worker boot is enough to prove which build is running; you do not need Assembly.LoadFrom for that.

sections.heading: internal versus InternalsVisibleTo
sections.prose: Default accessibility for a non-nested type is `internal`: visible inside this assembly only. Module 04 taught `private`/`protected` on members; friend assemblies sit one level up. `[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("Worker.Tests")]` grants that named assembly access to every `internal` type and member. Friendship is not transitive. If Tests is a friend of Worker, a helper assembly that references Tests still cannot touch Worker internals. If Worker is strong-named, the attribute must include the friend's public key (not version, culture, or public key token). Unsigned Worker uses the simple name only. This is how you keep CSV parser helpers `internal` while tests assert slicing behavior — without promoting the helper to public API. Do not InternalsVisibleTo a production sibling just to avoid designing a contract; that couples two deployables through a back door.

snippets.label: Friend tests without widening public surface
snippets.explanation: Tests can call RedisKeyFactory. Production hosts that only reference the public package cannot. Signed product assemblies need the test public key in the attribute string.

sections.heading: Metadata the loader already has
sections.prose: Every public and internal type is described in metadata whether you use reflection or not. Attributes, generic parameters, and method signatures are tables in the PE. That is why `typeof(T).Name` is cheap compared with `GetMethod` plus `Invoke`. Source generators (later in this module) read the same facts at compile time through Roslyn symbols instead of spinning up a runtime `Type`. When you explain a worker to an interviewer, separate three layers: C# source, assembly metadata, CLR execution. Confusing them is how people claim “C# is interpreted” or “internal is just a linter.”

interviewTakeaways: Assemblies are IL + metadata + manifest; NuGet packages ship those units, not TypeScript sources.
InternalsVisibleTo names a friend by simple name; signed assemblies also require the friend's public key.
Friendship is not transitive and does not replace a designed public contract between services.
commonPitfalls: Putting version or public key token in InternalsVisibleTo — the compiler wants name + public key for signed friends.
Making types public so tests compile instead of declaring a friend test assembly.
Assuming AssemblyC can see AssemblyA internals because it referenced friend AssemblyB.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node package exports hide files from importers. C# internal hides types from other assemblies; InternalsVisibleTo is an explicit exception, closer to a test-only export map than to `exports`.
